name: GizmoSQL
summary: A database server that wraps DuckDB (or SQLite) and serves it to many clients over Arrow Flight SQL, with TLS and authentication.
intro: DuckDB runs inside one program, and only one process can write to a database file. GizmoSQL is a server process that owns that DuckDB instance and lets many clients share it over the network. Clients speak Arrow Flight SQL, a gRPC protocol in which results travel as Arrow record batches, so DuckDB’s columnar output reaches the client without being turned into rows. The server listens on port 31337 with TLS or mutual TLS, password login and server-signed JWT tokens. Connect with JDBC, ADBC (Python, Go, C/C++, R), ODBC or the bundled `gizmosql_client` shell; adapters cover dbt, SQLMesh, Ibis, SQLAlchemy, Superset, Metabase, Grafana and Power BI. Whatever DuckDB can do, the server can do: query Parquet on object storage, attach DuckLake catalogs, load extensions. SQLite is a second, switchable backend. It ships as Docker images, Homebrew and Windows installers, a Kubernetes operator and an iOS app meant for demos.

GizmoData LLC sells it as open core. GizmoSQL Core is Apache 2.0 and free. Enterprise adds session instrumentation and `KILL SESSION`, per-catalog permissions, SSO through OIDC, statement queuing and Prometheus metrics, unlocked by a signed licence key, at $300 per vCPU per year with a $1,500 yearly minimum per server. GizmoData Cloud, launched in September 2026, runs managed clusters on AWS, Google Cloud and Azure on prepaid plans from $29 a month. The current release, v1.41.0, bundles DuckDB 1.5.6, with 1.4.5 on a long-term support channel.
strengths: Turns a DuckDB file into a shared network database with TLS and logins, in one container
Columnar Arrow Flight SQL on the wire, with JDBC, ADBC and ODBC drivers so BI tools and notebooks connect directly
Full DuckDB SQL and extensions: Parquet and S3, DuckLake catalogs, spatial
Apache 2.0 core that runs on Linux, macOS, Windows and Kubernetes
limits: Still one DuckDB on one machine: it scales up, not out
Operational controls such as SSO, per-catalog permissions, killing sessions, statement queuing and metrics are Enterprise only, billed per vCPU
The licence has moved before: it needed a licence key for production use until June 2025, and Enterprise code is proprietary
A small, founder-led vendor; Philip Moore wrote most of the commits
DuckDB now has its own server protocol, Quack; in the DuckDB team’s benchmark it moved 60 million rows in 4.9 s, against 17.4 s through GizmoSQL

items.name: GizmoSQL Enterprise
items.text: Core plus SSO, per-catalog permissions, session instrumentation and `KILL SESSION`, statement queuing and Prometheus metrics. Minimum $1,500 a year per server. You run it, with a licence key.

items.name: GizmoData Cloud
items.text: Managed GizmoSQL clusters on AWS, Google Cloud or Azure. The plan fee (Starter $29, Team $99, Business $499 a month) comes back as compute credit billed by the hour; managed storage is $0.05 per GB-month.

story: Arrow Flight SQL gave databases a way to send query results as columnar Arrow data instead of row by row. In April 2022 Tom Drabas at Voltron Data started an example Flight SQL server with SQLite and DuckDB backends. Philip Moore, a long-time data engineer then at Voltron Data, did most of the later work, and the example grew into a project called SQLFlite.

DuckDB’s in-process design left no built-in way for many users to share one database over a network. In October 2024 Moore forked SQLFlite under his own company, GizmoData, as GizmoSQL. At first it was a licensed product that printed a warning when run without a key. In June 2025 he made it open source under Apache 2.0, and in January 2026 added a separate, proprietary Enterprise edition. GizmoData Cloud, a managed version, followed in September 2026. By then DuckDB had shipped its own client-server protocol, Quack, citing Flight SQL servers among the workarounds people had built.

choices.choice: Arrow Flight SQL instead of the PostgreSQL wire protocol
choices.why: DuckDB already produces Arrow data. Sending Arrow batches over gRPC keeps results columnar end to end, and the Arrow project supplies JDBC and ADBC drivers.

choices.choice: One server process that owns the database
choices.why: Only one process can write to a DuckDB file. A server that holds the single instance lets many clients read and write through it.

choices.choice: Open core, with paid features in a separate directory
choices.why: Core stays Apache 2.0, while enterprise controls live in `src/enterprise/` under a commercial licence and unlock with a signed key.

timeline.text: Voltron Data starts a Flight SQL server example on DuckDB and SQLite
Philip Moore forks it as GizmoSQL in October, as a licensed product
GizmoSQL becomes open source under Apache 2.0 in June
Proprietary Enterprise edition in January; DuckDB ships Quack in May
